title: Express Basics
subtitle: Routing, middleware, and JSON APIs with the Express framework
author: KERNAL Team

whyItExists.problem: The raw http module requires manual routing, body parsing, error handling, and header management for every endpoint. Building a real API this way is tedious and error-prone.
whyItExists.solution: Express is a minimal web framework that adds: declarative routing (app.get/post/put/delete), middleware (app.use), body parsing (express.json()), and error handling with a consistent interface. It's the most popular Node.js framework.
whyItExists.whenToUse: REST APIs, web apps, backend services. Express is the industry standard for Node.js HTTP servers — huge ecosystem of compatible middleware.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: For extremely high throughput (Fastify is faster). For TypeScript-first codebases (NestJS provides better types). For serverless (use the native handler shape — though express works with serverless-http).

explainModes.beginner: Express makes building web servers much easier. Instead of manually checking req.url and req.method, you write app.get('/users', handler) and Express calls your handler when a GET request comes to /users. Middleware functions (app.use()) run before your handlers and can add features like JSON body parsing.
explainModes.simple: const app = express(); app.use(express.json()). Routes: app.get(path, handler), app.post(path, handler), app.put(path, handler), app.delete(path, handler). Route params: app.get('/users/:id', (req,res)=>{ req.params.id }). Query strings: req.query.name. Request body: req.body (after express.json()). Send JSON: res.json(obj). Status: res.status(404).json({error:'Not found'}). Listen: app.listen(3000, callback).
explainModes.standard: Middleware chain: app.use(fn) registers middleware that runs for every request. Middleware signature: (req, res, next) — call next() to pass to the next middleware. Order matters: middleware runs in registration order. Router: express.Router() groups routes — useful for /api/users routes in a separate file. Error middleware: 4-argument function (err, req, res, next) — catches errors thrown in route handlers. express.static('public') serves files. app.locals for app-wide variables.
explainModes.technical: req.params vs req.query vs req.body: params are in the URL path (/users/:id → req.params.id), query strings are after ? (/users?role=admin → req.query.role), body is the request payload (req.body after express.json()). Async route handlers: Express 4 doesn't auto-catch Promise rejections — wrap in try/catch or use express-async-errors. Express 5 (RC) adds async error propagation. Route chaining: app.route('/users').get(handler).post(handler). app.param() for param preprocessing.
explainModes.deepDive: Express middleware is just a function — it can read/modify req and res, end the request, or call next(). next(error) jumps to error-handling middleware. Layer: Express stores routes and middleware as an array of Layer objects. When a request comes in, Express walks the array and calls each matching layer. Route matching: Express uses the path-to-regexp library to convert route patterns ('/users/:id') to RegExps. Performance: Express adds ~1ms overhead per request (middleware traversal) compared to raw http. Fastify uses a Radix trie for route matching — O(log n) vs O(n) — much faster for many routes.

content.text: Call next() in every middleware that isn't an endpoint. If you forget, the request hangs — no response is ever sent. This is the most common Express beginner mistake.

questions.question: What does `app.use(express.json())` do?
options: It makes Express return JSON responses by default
It registers middleware that parses incoming request bodies with Content-Type: application/json and sets req.body to the parsed object
It enables JSON logging for all requests
It converts all route handler return values to JSON automatically
questions.explanation: express.json() is a middleware function. When a request comes in with Content-Type: application/json, it reads the body stream, parses the JSON, and sets req.body to the resulting JavaScript object. Without it, req.body would be undefined. It's typically registered with app.use() near the top so it runs before any route handlers.

faq.q: What is the difference between app.use() and app.get()?
faq.a: app.use(path, fn) registers middleware that matches any HTTP method on any path (or the given prefix). app.get(path, fn) only matches GET requests to that exact path. app.use() is for cross-cutting concerns (logging, auth, body parsing); app.get/post/put/delete are for specific endpoints. Note: app.use('/api', router) mounts a router at a prefix — it matches any method and any sub-path.
